exam_guide_revision: Reviewed v5, 2026-09-26. This is a practical Data Structures & Algorithms track built around developer problems, code, performance, state, transfer, and pattern recognition.

learning_design.unlock_rule: All learning reveals are required. Each node moves quickly through a concrete problem, the obvious failure/waste, the maintained state or invariant that fixes it, the pattern name, a different real-world transfer, and one quick check.
learning_design.mastery_note: The goal is not to enjoy studying algorithms. The goal is to recognize the structure fast enough that an unfamiliar problem starts to look like a problem you have already solved.

authoring_notes: Anti-boring rule set: no optional reveals; no definition-first nodes; no university-course voice; no fake corporate narrative; start with code/data/workload; expose the waste or bug; name the useful state; then name the pattern; finish with transfer.

modules.title: Move pointers instead of restarting work

nodes.title: Sorted pair search: squeeze the impossible side away

reveal.text: Sorted job sizes must produce a pair that exactly fills a capacity, with O(1) extra space. You are learning to use sorted order to eliminate pair candidates from both ends instead of trying every pair.

spans.text: Sorted job sizes must produce a pair that exactly fills a capacity, with O(1) extra space.
You are learning to use sorted order to eliminate pair candidates from both ends instead of trying every pair

reveal.text: An all-pairs scan ignores the strongest fact you were given: the values are ordered. Takeaway: the baseline tests pairs that sorted order can rule out in bulk.

spans.text: the baseline tests pairs that sorted order can rule out in bulk

reveal.text: Compare smallest + largest. Too small? Only moving the left pointer up can increase the sum. Too large? Move the right pointer down. Takeaway: the still-possible interval between left and right.

spans.text: the still-possible interval between left and right

reveal.text: Opposing two pointers. Trigger: sorted data + a pair relation where moving one side changes the result monotonically

spans.text: Opposing two pointers
sorted data + a pair relation where moving one side changes the result monotonically

reveal.text: Reconciling two sorted ID lists also advances the side whose current value is smaller. Different output, same ordered-elimination instinct. Takeaway: order tells you which side cannot help and may be discarded.

spans.text: order tells you which side cannot help and may be discarded

reveal.text: Current sum is below target. Which pointer moves? Answer: The left pointer moves right to increase the sum.

spans.text: The left pointer moves right to increase the sum.

glossary.definition: A value, pair, range, or state that could still satisfy the problem until evidence rules it out.

nodes.title: In-place cleanup is easier when one pointer reads and one pointer owns the clean prefix

reveal.text: An array contains tombstoned records. Compact active records to the front, preserve their order, and use O(1) extra space. You are learning to separate 'what am I inspecting?' from 'where does the next kept item belong?'.

spans.text: An array contains tombstoned records. Compact active records to the front, preserve their order, and use O(1) extra space.
You are learning to separate 'what am I inspecting?' from 'where does the next kept item belong?'

prompts.label: ONE POINTER READS; ONE POINTER OWNS THE OUTPUT PREFIX

annotations.title: write marks the next output slot
annotations.explanation: Positions before write are already the stable compacted result.

reveal.text: Invariant: `records[:write]` is exactly the active records seen so far, in original order. Takeaway: read position + length of the valid compacted prefix.

spans.text: read position + length of the valid compacted prefix

reveal.text: Read/write pointers. Trigger: stable in-place filtering, compaction, or overwrite where input scan and output position differ

spans.text: Read/write pointers
stable in-place filtering, compaction, or overwrite where input scan and output position differ

reveal.text: Removing zeros in-place or filtering invalid tokens uses the same clean-prefix invariant. Takeaway: one cursor consumes input while another marks the next output slot.

spans.text: one cursor consumes input while another marks the next output slot

reveal.text: What does `write` mean after processing read index r? Answer: It is the length / next slot of the compacted valid prefix.

spans.text: It is the length / next slot of the compacted valid prefix.

nodes.title: A linked chain can reveal its own cycle without a visited set

reveal.text: Configuration states form a `next` chain. You must detect whether following `next` eventually loops, using O(1) extra memory. You are learning to use two pointers moving at different speeds to expose repeated position structure.

spans.text: Configuration states form a `next` chain. You must detect whether following `next` eventually loops, using O(1) extra memory.
You are learning to use two pointers moving at different speeds to expose repeated position structure

reveal.text: A visited set is easy and correct, but it uses O(n) extra memory. Takeaway: the requirement asks you to detect revisiting without storing every visited node.

spans.text: the requirement asks you to detect revisiting without storing every visited node

reveal.text: Move one pointer one step and another two steps. In a cycle, the faster pointer eventually laps the slower one. Takeaway: relative pointer positions rather than stored history.

spans.text: relative pointer positions rather than stored history

reveal.text: Fast/slow pointers. Trigger: a single-successor chain where you need cycle/middle/distance information with constant extra memory

spans.text: Fast/slow pointers
a single-successor chain where you need cycle/middle/distance information with constant extra memory

reveal.text: The same speed relationship can find a linked-list midpoint: fast reaches the end while slow advances half as far. Takeaway: relative speed encodes structure without storing every visited position.

spans.text: relative speed encodes structure without storing every visited position

reveal.text: If fast reaches `None`, is there a cycle? Answer: No — the chain terminates.

spans.text: No — the chain terminates.

nodes.title: Neighboring windows overlap almost completely — stop recomputing them

reveal.text: You need the request total for every 5-minute block in a per-minute array. You are learning to reuse the previous fixed-size window instead of summing the same values again.

spans.text: You need the request total for every 5-minute block in a per-minute array.
You are learning to reuse the previous fixed-size window instead of summing the same values again

prompts.label: ONLY TWO VALUES CHANGE WHEN THE WINDOW SLIDES

reveal.code:
window = sum(values[:k])
best = window
for right in range(k, len(values)):
    window += values[right]
    window -= values[right - k]
    best = max(best, window)

annotations.title: One value enters
annotations.explanation: Everything else was already in the previous window.

annotations.title: One value leaves
annotations.explanation: Remove only the outgoing edge of the old window.

reveal.text: Maintain the aggregate. Sliding by one position changes only the entering and leaving elements. Takeaway: the aggregate of the current k-sized contiguous window.

spans.text: the aggregate of the current k-sized contiguous window

reveal.text: Fixed sliding window. Trigger: every candidate is a contiguous window of the same known size

spans.text: Fixed sliding window
every candidate is a contiguous window of the same known size

reveal.text: Rolling sensor averages, 7-day totals, and k-character statistics all reuse the same overlap. Takeaway: neighboring fixed windows differ by one incoming and one outgoing item.

spans.text: neighboring fixed windows differ by one incoming and one outgoing item

reveal.text: What work turns O(k) per window into O(1) per slide? Answer: Subtract the outgoing value and add the incoming value.

spans.text: Subtract the outgoing value and add the incoming value.

nodes.title: Grow until the rule breaks; shrink only enough to repair it

reveal.text: Find the longest contiguous request run containing at most K distinct user IDs. You are learning to maintain a variable-size window when validity can be repaired by moving the left edge forward.

spans.text: Find the longest contiguous request run containing at most K distinct user IDs.
You are learning to maintain a variable-size window when validity can be repaired by moving the left edge forward

reveal.text: Restarting a fresh scan from every left position repeats almost the entire window history. Takeaway: overlapping candidate ranges are rebuilt instead of maintained.

spans.text: overlapping candidate ranges are rebuilt instead of maintained

reveal.text: Expand right and update counts. When distinct users exceed K, advance left and remove counts until the window is valid again. Takeaway: current window counts + a validity condition that can be restored by shrinking left.

spans.text: current window counts + a validity condition that can be restored by shrinking left

reveal.text: Variable sliding window. Trigger: contiguous interval + monotonic repair: adding right may violate, moving left can restore

spans.text: Variable sliding window
contiguous interval + monotonic repair: adding right may violate, moving left can restore

reveal.text: Longest substring with at most K distinct characters has the same state skeleton as user-ID bursts. Takeaway: expand one edge, repair with the other, reuse all overlapping state.

spans.text: expand one edge, repair with the other, reuse all overlapping state

reveal.text: When the window becomes invalid, do you reset both pointers? Answer: No — move only the left edge until the maintained condition is valid again.

spans.text: No — move only the left edge until the maintained condition is valid again.

nodes.title: Fixed window, variable window, or prefix state? The query tells you

reveal.text: Three workloads look like 'arrays': rolling 5-minute totals, longest valid burst, and thousands of arbitrary range sums. You are learning to choose the contiguous-range pattern from how the interval is defined and queried.

spans.text: Three workloads look like 'arrays': rolling 5-minute totals, longest valid burst, and thousands of arbitrary range sums.
You are learning to choose the contiguous-range pattern from how the interval is defined and queried

reveal.text: Using 'sliding window' for every contiguous problem leads to awkward or incorrect code, especially with arbitrary queries or negative values. Takeaway: surface similarity hides different state transitions.

spans.text: surface similarity hides different state transitions

reveal.text: Fixed size → fixed window. Expand/shrink validity → variable window. Many independent range queries → prefix state. Takeaway: how the candidate interval changes from one query/state to the next.

spans.text: how the candidate interval changes from one query/state to the next

reveal.text: Window/prefix discrimination. Trigger: the problem is contiguous but the relationship between neighboring candidates differs

spans.text: Window/prefix discrimination
the problem is contiguous but the relationship between neighboring candidates differs

reveal.text: This decision is more useful than memorizing example problem names because it survives new stories. Takeaway: candidate-update mechanics select the pattern.

spans.text: candidate-update mechanics select the pattern

reveal.text: Thousands of independent range sums on static data: window or prefix? Answer: Prefix state.

spans.text: Prefix state.

nodes.title: Intervals become simple after you line them up by start time

reveal.text: Maintenance windows arrive unsorted and overlapping. You need their combined occupied time blocks. You are learning to sort intervals once so overlap becomes a local comparison with the current merged interval.

spans.text: Maintenance windows arrive unsorted and overlapping. You need their combined occupied time blocks.
You are learning to sort intervals once so overlap becomes a local comparison with the current merged interval

reveal.text: Comparing every window with every other window creates messy global overlap logic. Takeaway: unsorted intervals make relevant neighbors hard to identify.

spans.text: unsorted intervals make relevant neighbors hard to identify

reveal.text: Sort by start. Keep one current merged interval. If the next start overlaps it, extend the end; otherwise emit current and start a new one. Takeaway: the current merged interval after processing all earlier starts.

spans.text: the current merged interval after processing all earlier starts

reveal.text: Sort + merge intervals. Trigger: the output is the union/consolidation of many intervals

spans.text: Sort + merge intervals
the output is the union/consolidation of many intervals

reveal.text: Calendar blocks, maintenance outages, and reserved IP ranges all use the same ordered-overlap scan. Takeaway: sorting turns global overlap into local adjacency.

spans.text: sorting turns global overlap into local adjacency

reveal.text: After sorting by start, what one interval do you need to carry? Answer: The current merged interval.

spans.text: The current merged interval.

nodes.title: Do touching intervals overlap? The product contract decides

reveal.text: Bookings use half-open `[start,end)` time ranges, so one booking ending at 10:00 and another starting at 10:00 can coexist. You are learning to make endpoint semantics explicit before writing overlap comparisons.

spans.text: Bookings use half-open `[start,end)` time ranges, so one booking ending at 10:00 and another starting at 10:00 can coexist.
You are learning to make endpoint semantics explicit before writing overlap comparisons

reveal.text: Using `next.start <= current.end` blindly can merge touching intervals even when the contract says end time is exclusive. Takeaway: one comparison operator silently changes the meaning of overlap.

spans.text: one comparison operator silently changes the meaning of overlap

reveal.text: Write the interval convention first. For half-open bookings, touching at the boundary is non-overlapping; for closed intervals it may count as overlap. Takeaway: the chosen endpoint convention and its exact overlap predicate.

spans.text: the chosen endpoint convention and its exact overlap predicate

reveal.text: Endpoint-aware interval reasoning. Trigger: start/end equality can change whether ranges conflict, merge, or touch

spans.text: Endpoint-aware interval reasoning
start/end equality can change whether ranges conflict, merge, or touch

reveal.text: Memory ranges, time bookings, array slices, and version intervals all need explicit endpoint semantics. Takeaway: boundary convention determines the correct comparison operators.

spans.text: boundary convention determines the correct comparison operators

reveal.text: For half-open `[a,b)` and `[b,c)`, do the intervals overlap? Answer: No.

spans.text: No.

glossary.definition: An interval [start, end) that includes the start boundary and excludes the end boundary.
An interval [start, end] that includes both endpoints.

nodes.title: The same intervals can require three different algorithms depending on the output

reveal.text: One dataset of bookings may be used to merge occupied time, detect any conflict, or compute maximum concurrent rooms. You are learning to choose interval state from the output rather than assuming 'interval problem = merge'.

spans.text: One dataset of bookings may be used to merge occupied time, detect any conflict, or compute maximum concurrent rooms.
You are learning to choose interval state from the output rather than assuming 'interval problem = merge'

reveal.text: Always merging destroys information needed for concurrency counts and does extra work if you only need a yes/no conflict. Takeaway: the input shape is the same but the requested output is different.

spans.text: the input shape is the same but the requested output is different

reveal.text: Ask what must be returned: union → sort/merge; any overlap → sorted neighbor check; peak concurrency → ordered start/end events or heap. Takeaway: the output contract, not merely the presence of intervals.

spans.text: the output contract, not merely the presence of intervals

reveal.text: Interval-problem discrimination. Trigger: multiple interval algorithms are plausible but answer different questions

spans.text: Interval-problem discrimination
multiple interval algorithms are plausible but answer different questions

reveal.text: Calendar conflict checking and room-count scheduling share input data but need different maintained state. Takeaway: output semantics choose the interval algorithm.

spans.text: output semantics choose the interval algorithm

reveal.text: Need only whether any two bookings conflict. Must you build the full merged union? Answer: No — after sorting, a neighbor overlap check can be enough.

spans.text: No — after sorting, a neighbor overlap check can be enough.
